exercises.prompt: Implement row_sums(matrix), where matrix is a list of rows and each row is a list of numbers, so it returns a list with the sum of each row — row_sums([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) is [3, 7]. Rows may have different lengths, an empty row sums to 0, and an empty matrix returns an empty list.
exercises.solution:
def row_sums(matrix):
    return [sum(row) for row in matrix]
hints: You want one number per row, so iterate the outer list and collapse each row to a single value.
sum(row) totals one row; since a row is itself a list, sum handles it directly, and an empty row sums to 0.

exercises.prompt: Implement flatten(matrix) so it merges the rows of matrix into one list, one level deep — flatten([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The elements keep their left-to-right order, an empty row contributes nothing, and an empty matrix returns an empty list.
exercises.solution:
def flatten(matrix):
    return [x for row in matrix for x in row]
hints: Flattening visits every element of every row and drops them into one flat list — two loops, the outer over rows and the inner over each row's items.
A comprehension can stack both loops in order: [x for row in matrix for x in row], read left to right.
return [x for row in matrix for x in row] — an empty row contributes nothing, so ragged input is fine.

exercises.prompt: Implement pair_up(a, b) so it pairs the two lists element-wise into a list of (a_i, b_i) tuples — pair_up([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) is [(1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6)]. If the lists differ in length, stop at the shorter one. Two empty lists return an empty list.
exercises.solution:
def pair_up(a, b):
    return list(zip(a, b))
hints: zip walks two lists in lockstep, handing you one element from each at a time.
list(zip(a, b)) builds the list of pairs, and zip stops as soon as the shorter list runs out.
return list(zip(a, b)) — each pair comes back as a tuple, like (1, 4).

exercises.prompt: Implement column_at(matrix, c) so it returns column c of the matrix as a list — the element at index c taken from each row. column_at([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], 0) is [1, 3, 5]. Assume every row has an element at index c. An empty matrix returns an empty list.
exercises.solution:
def column_at(matrix, c):
    return [row[c] for row in matrix]
hints: A column is one element taken from every row, so produce one value per row.
Take index c from each row: row[c].

exercises.prompt: Implement transpose(matrix) so it swaps the rows and columns of a rectangular matrix: the first row of the result gathers the first element of every original row, and so on. transpose([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) is [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]. Each new row is a list. Assume the matrix has at least one row, every row has the same length, and that length is at least one.
exercises.solution:
def transpose(matrix):
    return [list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)]
hints: The result has one row per original column, and each new row gathers that column's value from every original row.
zip(*matrix) feeds each row into zip as a separate argument, so the tuples it yields are the columns; wrap each in list to make it a row.
return [list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)] — the star unpacks the rows so zip can line up the columns.
